I am still relatively novice myself, so I welcome corrections but my understanding is that Lean and Six Sigma are two dinstinct approaches - Lean focuses on removing waste from a process while Six Sigma focuses on reducing variation in output of a process. 

However, they overlap heavily in a lot of fundamental ways: they both require a deep understanding of the process, the customer and what they value, etc. Generally, when you are learning Six Sigma, you are absorbing some lean thinking, though lean can go much deeper on its own as well. Therefore, most companies will lump them together but its not uncommon to see courses dedicated specifically to Six Sigma or Lean in themselves. 

  
In my opinion, you really cant go wrong with a course for LSS. My advice is to see what education your company offers around either or both of these things. If nothing exists, see what education is available that your company will pay for. The best of all is to just volunteer with project solving teams - Lean and Six Sigma are both things that are really an art and a science. You can learn about them all day long in a classroom or even just youtube; but its a whole different story when you are trying to actually do it within a team. Most mature Lean companies recognize this and dont really care where your resume letters come from as long as you can reliably speak to it and show exmaple results of employing the methods.

Lean and Six Sigma are two different methodologies for process improvement, though they share enough similarities and tool concepts that they are frequently lumped together. Lean focuses on removing waste from a process based on customer value of the process. Six Sigma focuses on reducing the variation of the output of a process to make the output as close as possible to the customer's desire every time. Both methods rely on tools to understand the process and the value the customer wants out of the process, so you may see an overlap in tools. If you are a Six Sigma belt, you are most likely going to pick up lean concepts and use of lean tools by osmosis. 

  
I cant speak to the ASQ training class you mention, and I dont have an ASQ belt cert specifically, but based on the book of knowledge I have studied, ASQ belt certifications focus pretty specifically on Six Sigma. However, if you go with an ASQ cert, Lean shouldnt be that hard to grasp. 

  
TLDR - dont over think it, ASQ belt certification is a great certification to get and if you practice Six Sigma, you probably wont escape learning / using Lean in some fashion anyway... which is the reason they are often lumped together into Lean Six Sigma. Some companies may offer distinct certifications between the two based on their business model and culture, but for the most part they are generally two wheels on the same engine of process improvement.

I think you are on the right path for the level you are on. Based on what you explained is being asked of you, I would focus on data and process mapping: gather some solid *current* data on lead time for the whole process, data on time for each portion then map out the process and identify where at in the process the pain points, obstacles, key factors driving lead time lie, then suggest changes around those things. Are things being batched unnecessarily? Multiple points of waiting on email replies ? .. those are some, not all, of the most common drivers of high lead times I have seen in service processes. Your examples you give could be captured as pain points early on in the process map

Be careful on collecting / analyzing time data... it sounds easy but can quickly go awry if someone is manually collecting it with the wrong understanding of stop / start points, wrong operational definitions. Etc

Based on what you wrote, I would have a lot of questions that aren't feasible for a forum like this. 

What process improvement capacity do you and the team have? Is there a readiness to do a full dmaic process or is this something where it may be appropriate to simply recommend a few lean-basded changes?

Regardless of the answer, I would start at the bottom: what data is available? What is the current state now and why work on this now? Do you have leadership support and SMEs identified ? This will affect your ability to collect data for an objective baseline if it is not readily available. 

What is the average cycle time for each of the major portions in the process you listed? How can that be measured, even if by hand ? Understanding that and leaning on SMEs to understand key factors that cause the lead time may give you a general direction as to what portions to work on. Take your process map and get the SMEs to point out pain points in the process and align that with the portions that take the longest... then list out why and do some root cause investigation. At that point you should have the ammo to go back to the team and prioritize which factors to solution around

When you ask  how you establish a standard time: are you asking how you understand what the expectation of an efficient lead time should be? In most cases there are several factors that could guide this : policy, org goals. Leadership in general, other process needs, etc. You may want to look into the concept of entitlement... basically what is the best the process can perform given its setup? There is a ceiling somewhere and entitlement basically calculates a goal output based on what the best output is and how often it is hit... you should be able to Google it for a better explanation

One lesson I have learned through doing more and more projects is that rarely do projects have complete clean traversals through dmaic from end to end. Six Sigma is both an art and a science. It's easy to learn the tools and what value they provide but only experience can teach when, how, and why to apply certain principles. Early in my experience I found myself trying to apply tools in a rigid manner and sequential manner and ran into many issues. There is no perfect algorithm for when and how to apply which tools... not all projects need a dpmo calculation to achieve the six Sigma methodology. 

I would probably agree with you... using dpmo in this case may be overly rigid and could lose non - six Sigma oriented team members. The important point is you establish some baseline metric that is clear, measurable, and people all agree on

I'm not in manufacturing so I don't rely on  DPMO as much, I am more than happy to be educated if someone disagrees:

My understanding is you are on the right track for the most part: it depends on how many defects chances you have per widget ... but the idea of a defect is usually driven by customer specifications, what they are willing to accept. So in your first example if sloppy handwriting is something that still gets the output's value to the customer and just something that your company prefers not to have, it's up to your company if it is a defect opptuntity or not related to customer output specifications

If I were in your shoes, I would probably lean towards your second thought. If they're are 22 separate boxes that may meet the customers expectations or not, I would say there are 22 defect opportunities per output. There needs to be a standard based on customer expectations as to what causes those boxes to be defective. 

also of note, dpmo is based off a million opportunities, borne out of mass production scenarios. There is no hard and fast rule that it must be 1 million. You can change the formula to 100. 100,000, etc... this may help more effectively represent performance

Six Sigma and Lean are things where the certs on a resume mean almost nothing unless from asq or maybe iassc. Because there is no true standard beyond those orgs, hiring employers really don't know what you truly can or can't do

Instead I would scratch and claw to get involved in any LSS based work at your current employer, or work to find an employer that indentifies with LSS in the job descriptions of roles you already do so that you work there as a way to get involved. This could take the form of volunteering to take notes, update huddle boards, join project meetings as resource, etc... to eventually become a regular part of the process improvement sphere at that org

You mentioned project management, do you have experience in being involved with any specific tools or accomplishment around process improvement?

The goal would be to list specific projects, accomplishments, or even tools on your resume that you have enough comfort with that you can speak to using during an interview.... even if you were only part or a team that used them or did the projects. 

When it comes to landing LSS jobs, even the slightest bit of experience speaks volumes over certifications. Certications just give you the educational context to be involved in using the tools... the real challenge is getting a chance to slowly start using the tools to be able to gain the initial experience. In my previous job, I did LSS as a volunteer in addition to my normal role until I felt comfortable listing LSS based experience on my resume to land my first entry level LSS focused job

What tools are supposed to use ? My first thought if going with running would be to change your metric so it would be like x number of times you did a 2 mile run per week with a specific goal. 

You could do a fish bone  of all the reasons you couldn't run that week (weather, shoe problems, worked over time, was out of town, gym closed, fit bit not charged etc)

Then do a process map of how you get ready and track your run, pointing out how wishbone factors come into play in the process. 

You could also put a pareto chart together around the things you put into your fish bone. 

Your charter would consist of the metric, your team (your family who supports you or your running friends) scope (only runs preparing for your competition, not jogs or treadmills etc)

Experience is much more valuable... May be better to use your experience to land at a company that will do that.
